pos.personaBrief: Cullis valued possession only as the means of getting the ball forward ('we cannot send it back into their defensive area until we have possession'); the Sports Argus contrasted Wolves using the long pass 'all the time' with Honved waiting 'until the set-up is right'. Danger and speed, not keeping the ball, defined control.

pro.personaBrief: Cullis's own principle was that 'every pass is if possible decisive and long rather than pretty and short' and that the ball should reach the opponents' box 'in a maximum of three passes', with quick distribution from defence and long balls from the keeper (Reep).

est.personaBrief: A standard W-M with fixed positional labels (Honved line-up), wingers kept on the touchline (Broadbent used 'as an advanced winger lying on the touchline') and long balls into space for onrushing wingers, i.e. a spread, positional shape rather than tight combinations.

lar.personaBrief: Wingers were central to the method: Mullen and Hancocks were 'the kind of wingers I considered essential to successful football', firing crosses into the area, with full-backs instructed to find a forward and even Broadbent pushed out to the touchline.

blo.personaBrief: Cullis demanded 'rapid tackling by every player so that we obtain possession of the ball before the other side has it under control' and a high-tempo game that 'would pressure opponents into mistakes', within a W-M noted for defensive resilience.

mar.personaBrief: No source states the scheme; the W-M of the era assigned direct opponents and the aggressive tackling-everywhere demand points man-oriented, while Cullis blaming Wright for being drawn 'too far forward' v Honved shows the centre-half was meant to hold position rather than chase.

pla.personaBrief: Flowers: 'our manager never sets out to copy the tactics of any other club' and 'the Wolves plan is a simple one to follow'; Hooper was dropped for not carrying out 'our tactical principles'. Even against Honved he kept the long-ball style, changing only the pitch conditions and talking to Wright at half-time.

res.personaBrief: Cullis said the primary duty is to entertain, but defined it as the Wolverhampton public demanding 'that Wolves should score at least one more goal than their opponents'; the side played 'a doctrine of all-out attack' and accepted the 'kick-and-rush' label for its efficiency.

sis.personaBrief: The system came first: an 'ideal winger' (Hooper) was released for not fitting the tactical principles, every player had fitness targets and tackling duties, and the plan was simple and uniform for all.

jog.personaBrief: 'Cullis placed huge emphasis on fitness and power', 'train until it hurts', a tempo 'beyond the capacity of the other side' and a style relying on 'fitness, pace and aggression', though ball players like Broadbent still had a place.

bas.personaBrief: Cullis drew on the Wath Wanderers nursery (Swinbourne), signed Broadbent at 17, won the 1958 FA Youth Cup with the 'Cullis Cubs' and released veteran Hancocks 'to prepare for the future', though established men like Wright still blocked youth captain Palin.

lid.personaBrief: 'A strict disciplinarian throughout his managerial career' who wanted 'far more iron than velvet in your touch', with Buckley's strict discipline; Flowers notes he avoided big inquests after bad games, but authority, not consultation, was the base.
